title: Basil's new city
hookLine: Basil of Caesarea built a place of care for the poor and sick, and his friend called it a new city

lines: I WILL PULL DOWN MY BARNS.
SOMETHING ON THE EDGE OF TOWN.
cards: "I will pull down my barns, and build greater." That's the rich man in one of Jesus' parables, in Luke's Gospel. His harvest is huge, so he plans bigger storage, and that night his life is asked of him.
Basil, then a priest in Caesarea, in what's now central Turkey, and later its bishop, preached on that line to his own people.
In his time, a famine came to his city, and the rich, like the man in the parable, had full barns. Basil had a sermon, a pulpit, and a gift for making people uncomfortable.
By the end he's built, on the edge of town, what his close friend would call a new city.

teach.h: THE FAMINE: HE SERVED WITH HIS HANDS.
teach.b: The famine first. His friend Gregory tells it, in a speech in Basil's memory. Basil opened the storehouses of those who had them, by the force of his preaching.
He gathered the hungry in one place and served them himself, with his own hands, alongside his helpers. In his sermon on the barns, Basil pushes hard.

teach.h: THE BREAD YOU KEEP IS THE HUNGRY'S.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the bread you keep in store belongs to the hungry; the coat in your closet belongs to the one without one. He isn't asking for leftovers. He's asking whose the extra really is.

teach.h: LODGING, FOOD, NURSING, ON THE EDGE.
teach.b: Outside Caesarea, Basil put up a whole complex: lodging for travelers and strangers, a place for the poor, care for the sick, with people to nurse them and workers to keep it going. A local governor was apparently uneasy.
Basil wrote to him: what harm does this do the state? We're housing strangers and caring for the sick.
Go a little way out of the city, Gregory says in paraphrase, and look at the new city, a storehouse of devotion, where the rich put their surplus.

And he singles out the people others avoided: those with the disease that disfigured skin and drove sufferers out of town. Basil didn't keep his distance. He greeted them, embraced them, even kissed them, as brothers.

teach.h: HE KISSED THE ONES SENT AWAY.
teach.b: Not a building, but a bishop bending down to kiss someone everyone else had sent away.

how: Churches and Christian orders run hospitals, clinics, hospices, shelters and food banks, and church members give to and volunteer in them.

o: the rich man in Jesus' parable who pulled down his barns to build more
a governor who worried about a new city outside Caesarea
a bishop who built a place of care for strangers and the sick

in his sermon on the rich man's barns.

games.q: you're Basil. a governor is uneasy about your new buildings outside town. what do you do?
o: tear them down to keep the peace.
write to him: what harm does it do to house strangers and nurse the sick?
games.why: Basil wrote to defend it, describing the lodging for strangers and the care for the sick.

practice: Bring to mind a place near you where people are cared for when sick or poor, a clinic, a hospice, a shelter, a food bank, and remember it if it ever carried you.

Basil asked his governor what harm the place did; ask instead what it runs short of, blankets, cans, a driver, a thank-you for the night staff. If you pray, pray for the sick there and those who care for them.

wordCard.voice: Basil. The bishop of Caesarea who built a place of care outside his town, for strangers, the poor and the sick, that his friend Gregory called a new city.

carryVoice: Your line: a city of mercy. Built just outside the city. That's day seven hundred seventy-three.
